heading: Preamble
text: NIGERIA REVENUE SERVICE REVENUE HOUSE, PLOT 1241, KUR MOHAMMED AVENUE, CENTRAL AREA, ABUJA, NIGERIA INFORMATION CIRCULAR NO: 2026/18 PUBLICATION DATE: 29TH JUNE, 2026 Subject: GUIDELINES ON THE WITHHOLDING OF VALUE ADDED TAX

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/18: Guidelines on the Withholding of Value Added Tax
heading: Introduction
text: 1.0 Introduction These Guidelines are issued by the Nigeria Revenue Service (“the Service”) to provide clarity on the implementation of the provisions relating to Withholding of Value Added Tax (VAT). They set out the obligations, procedures and compliance requirements for all relevant stakeholders including non-resident suppliers, taxable persons, appointed agents, and government entities in respect of the deduction, remittance, and reporting of VAT on taxable supplies. This circular withdraws and replaces the earlier FIRS Information Circular No: 2023/14 of 29th December, 2023

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/18: Guidelines on the Withholding of Value Added Tax
heading: Legal Framework
text: 2.0 Legal Framework The Nigeria Tax Act (NTA), 2025 provides as follows: Section 150 (3) empowers the Service to appoint any person including a non-resident supplier of taxable goods to deduct or withhold VAT; and the person so appointed is required to remit the VAT deducted or withheld to the Service in the currency of transaction. Section 150(4) provides that where a person appointed as an agent for the collection of VAT makes a taxable supply to a person in Nigeria, the taxable person shall not have the obligation to withhold, except where the appointed agent fails to collect the VAT. Section 154 (1) mandates all Federal, State, Local Government and their respective Ministries, Department & Agencies (MDAs) to collect or withhold VAT on taxable supplies (all payments) made to contractors and remit same to the Service. Section 154 (3) requires the persons obligated to withhold VAT to submit returns, accompanied with a schedule showing the name, Tax ID and address of the contractor or supplier, invoice number, gross amount of invoice, amount of the VAT and the month to which the return relates.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/18: Guidelines on the Withholding of Value Added Tax
heading: Withholding of VAT on Taxable Supplies Received
text: 3.0 Withholding of VAT on Taxable Supplies Received An appointed agent having the obligation to withhold the VAT charged on invoices of taxable supplies received (including works, services, goods, etc.) shall withhold and remit same to the Service in line with these Guidelines. This is in addition to their existing obligation to collect and remit VAT on their taxable supplies. The suppliers (service providers, contractors, vendors, etc.) must state separately, the gross amount of taxable supplies, VAT rate, and the amount of VAT charged on each invoice (including bill, debit note or any such document employed to record the transaction).

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/18: Guidelines on the Withholding of Value Added Tax
heading: Obligation to Withhold VAT from Suppliers
text: 4.0 Obligation to Withhold VAT from Suppliers An appointed agent shall have the following obligations: a. deduct or withhold VAT stated on the invoice issued by their suppliers, vendors or contractors (the VAT shall not be paid to the supplier); b. prepare a schedule showing the name, Tax ID, and address of the contractor or supplier, invoice number, gross amount of invoice, amount of the VAT, and the month to which the return relates; c. remit the amount withheld to the Service on or before the 14th day of the month immediately following the month of the transaction; and d. file the returns of VAT withheld using the appropriate fields in NRS tax administration solution.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/18: Guidelines on the Withholding of Value Added Tax
heading: Taxable supplies between companies having obligations to
text: 4.1 Taxable supplies between companies having obligations to withhold VAT Where a company having the obligation to withhold VAT makes taxable supplies to another company having a similar obligation to withhold VAT, the recipient of the supplies (the purchaser) shall account for the VAT on the transaction in line with these Guidelines. Where a non-resident supplier, appointed pursuant to Section 150(3) of the NTA, makes a taxable supply to an appointed agent in Nigeria, the appointed non-resident supplier shall have the primary responsibility to collect the tax due and remit same to the Service. However, where the appointed non-resident person fails to collect the tax, the Nigerian appointed agent shall withhold the VAT in line with these Guidelines and remit same to the Service. In the case of supply by a non-resident person not appointed, the taxable person to whom the supply is made in Nigeria, including an appointed agent in Nigeria, shall have the obligation to withhold the tax in line with these Guidelines.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/18: Guidelines on the Withholding of Value Added Tax
heading: Accounting for VAT Withheld
text: 5.0 Accounting for VAT Withheld A taxable person having the obligation to withhold VAT shall: a. maintain an account, referred to as “VAT Withheld Account” in its book or ledger, separate from its VAT Accounts; b. record to the credit of the “VAT Withheld Account” all VAT withheld from suppliers; c. record to the debit of the “VAT Withheld Account” all sums remitted to the Service, being VAT withheld from suppliers; and d. make the statement of the “VAT Withheld Account” available for audit, from time to time, as may be required by the Service.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/18: Guidelines on the Withholding of Value Added Tax
heading: Error or omission on remittance schedule
text: 6.0 Error or omission on remittance schedule A taxable person having obligation to withhold VAT shall ensure that the field to be populated on the schedules of suppliers to be uploaded on the NRS tax administration solution are done accurately and correctly, to avoid giving unintended credit to a wrong person (i.e. suppliers). A taxable person or appointed agent can revisit the uploaded schedule of suppliers to effect corrections where necessary.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/18: Guidelines on the Withholding of Value Added Tax
heading: Filing Obligation
text:
7.0 VAT Returns
7.1 Filing Obligation An appointed agent shall file a separate VAT return in respect of the VAT withheld to the Service on or before the 14th day of the following month in the currency of the transaction.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/18: Guidelines on the Withholding of Value Added Tax
heading: Mode of Filing Returns
text: 7.2 Mode of Filing Returns The returns for VAT withheld should be filed using the relevant module on the NRS tax administration solution or any format as may be prescribed by the Service. Taxpayers are to be on-boarded on the VAT e-invoicing when required by the Service.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/18: Guidelines on the Withholding of Value Added Tax
heading: Remittance of VAT withheld
text: 7.3 Remittance of VAT withheld a. VAT withheld should be remitted separately from VAT collected on supplies; and b. VAT should be remitted in the currency in which it was assessed.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/18: Guidelines on the Withholding of Value Added Tax
heading: Input Tax of Withheld Output Tax
text: 8.0 Input Tax of Withheld Output Tax lnput VAT incurred on taxable supplies can be deducted from the output VAT or tax payable in line with the provisions of Section 155 (5) of NTA. In the event that the output tax has been withheld by a company covered under paragraph 2.0 of this Guideline, the supplier: a. shall disclose the total output tax collectible on all its supplies in the VAT returns for the relevant month; b. shall deduct output tax withheld at source from the total output tax reported in its VAT return for the relevant month to arrive at a net output tax (i.e., output tax collected); c. shall, in arriving at the VAT payable, deduct input tax on all supplies from the net output tax, including input tax relating to the supplies for which output tax was withheld; and d. where the input VAT exceeds the net output VAT, may utilise the amount refundable to offset future VAT liability or request for a refund.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/18: Guidelines on the Withholding of Value Added Tax
heading: Refund of Input Tax
text: 9.0 Refund of Input Tax Where a taxpayer covered under paragraph 2.0 of this Guideline requests for a refund, the Service shall treat the request in accordance with the Guidelines on Tax Refund.

heading: Offences and Penalties
text: 10.0 Offences and Penalties The penalties stipulated under the relevant provisions of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act shall apply to any person who fails to comply with the obligations set out in these Guidelines.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/21: Guidelines on the Taxation of Virtual Assets
heading: Preamble
text: NIGERIA REVENUE SERVICE PLOT 1241, KUR MOHAMMED AVENUE, CENTRAL AREA, ABUJA, NIGERIA INFORMATION CIRCULAR NO. 2026/21 PUBLICATION DATE: 31st July 2026 SUBJECT: GUIDELINES ON THE TAXATION OF VIRTUAL ASSETS These Guidelines are issued for the information and guidance of taxpayers, Virtual Asset Service Providers (VASPs), Peer-to-Peer (P2P) marketplace operators, tax consultants, financial institutions, and all persons engaged in Virtual Assets (VA) activities.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/21: Guidelines on the Taxation of Virtual Assets
heading: Introduction
text: 1.0 Introduction These Guidelines have been developed to establish a clear and standardised framework for the tax administration of VA and VA transactions in Nigeria.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/21: Guidelines on the Taxation of Virtual Assets
heading: Purpose
text: 2.0 Purpose The purpose of these guidelines is to provide an administrative guide on the taxation of VAs in Nigeria, including - (a) the tax obligations of persons engaged in VAs transactions; (b) the registration, reporting, filing and record keeping obligations applicable to taxpayers and VAs service providers; (c) the valuation and computation of taxable income arising from VAs transactions; and (d) clarity in the administration and enforcement of the tax laws relating to VA.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/21: Guidelines on the Taxation of Virtual Assets
heading: Legal Framework
text: 3.0 Legal Framework (a) Section 4 of the Nigeria Revenue Service Establishment Act, 2025; (b) Ninth Schedule to the Nigeria Tax Act, 2025 (the “NTA”); (c) Section 79 and the Fifth Schedule to the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025 (the “NTAA”); and (d) Any relevant provision under the above-mentioned Acts relating to VAs.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/21: Guidelines on the Taxation of Virtual Assets
heading: Scope of application
text: 4.0 Scope of application These Guidelines apply to any person who - (a) acquires, disposes of, exchanges or otherwise deals in VA; 1 | Pa ge (b) receives income or any payment in the form of VA; (c) operates as a VASP and P2P marketplace; (d) derives income, profits or gains from VAs that is liable to tax in Nigeria; or (e) provides services relating to VA.

heading: Applicable Taxes
text: 6.0 Applicable Taxes VA transactions shall be subject to the applicable taxes imposed under the NTA. A single transaction may give rise to more than one tax liability such as income tax, VAT or stamp duty, where different taxable events arise from the same transaction.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/21: Guidelines on the Taxation of Virtual Assets
heading: Income Tax of Individuals
text:
6.1 Income tax
6.1.1 Income Tax of Individuals (1) A resident individual who derives income, profits or gains from VA transactions shall be liable to income tax of individuals in accordance with the provisions of the NTA. (2) Income liable to tax includes — (a) gains realised on the disposal of VA; (b) employment income received in VA; (c) professional or consultancy fees received in VA; (d) business income received in VA; 3 | Pa ge (e) mining rewards; (f) staking rewards; (g) decentralised finance (DeFi) rewards; (h) yield on investment; (i) liquidity mining incentives; (j) protocol rewards; (k) royalties received in VA; (l) airdrops and hard fork distributions that constitute taxable income; and (m) every other income arising from VA activities that is chargeable to tax under the NTA. (3) Income shall be recognised at the FMV of the VA on the date the taxpayer acquires unrestricted ownership or control of the asset. (4) Taxpayers shall declare such income in their annual income tax returns together with any supporting documentation prescribed by the relevant tax authority. (5) Where VA are received as employment income or emoluments, the employer shall report the remuneration in VA and the quantity paid, together with its FMV in USD as at the date of payment, in accordance with section 14 of the NTAA.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/21: Guidelines on the Taxation of Virtual Assets
heading: Income Tax of Companies
text: 6.1.2 Income Tax of Companies (1) A company that derives profits from VA transactions shall be liable to income tax of companies under the NTA. (2) Taxable profits include all income and gains derived from VA, including income and gains from— (a) trading in VA; (b) operation of VA exchanges; (c) transaction fees charged by VASPs; (d) brokerage commissions; (e) custody services; (f) wallet administration services; (g) token issuance activities; (h) mining operations; (i) staking activities; (j) decentralised finance activities; (k) investment gains; and (l) any other income or profit arising from VA business activities. (3) The taxable profits of a company shall be computed in accordance with the relevant provisions of the NTA. 4 | Pa ge (4) VASPs, like every other company, shall bear their own corporate income tax liability on their revenues. This is separate from their deduction of tax at source obligations.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/21: Guidelines on the Taxation of Virtual Assets
heading: Non-resident
text: 6.1.3 Non-resident (1) A non-resident person that derives income, profits or gains from VA activities in Nigeria shall be liable to tax in accordance with the relevant provisions of the NTA and the NTAA. (2) The provisions relating to Significant Economic Presence (SEP) and Nigerian-source income shall apply to VA activities in the same manner as they apply to any other taxable business. (3) The tax liability and other obligations of non-resident persons in Nigeria are set out in the Information Circular on Taxation of Non-Resident Persons and Guidelines for Filing Income Tax Returns by Foreign Companies, both at www.nrs.gov.ng/resources.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/21: Guidelines on the Taxation of Virtual Assets
heading: Value Added Tax (VAT)
text: 6.2 Value Added Tax (VAT) (1) The transfer of ownership of a VA shall not, of itself, constitute a taxable supply for VAT purposes. (2) VAT shall, however, apply to taxable supplies connected with VA transactions including— (a) exchange fees charged by VASPs; (b) brokerage commissions; (c) custody fees; (d) wallet management fees; (e) listing fees; (f) transaction facilitation fees; (g) advisory services; (h) digital platform service fees; (i) professional services rendered in connection with VA; and (j) every other taxable service supplied for consideration. (3) Where VAs are used as consideration for taxable goods or services, VAT shall apply to the underlying supply in the same manner as if payment had been made in fiat currency. (4) The supplier shall account for and remit VAT in accordance with the applicable tax laws. 5 | Pa ge (5) Where a non-resident VASP supplies taxable digital services to persons in Nigeria, the provider shall comply with the registration and compliance obligations applicable to non-resident suppliers. (6) Where a non-resident supplier does not charge VAT, the resident company is required to self-charge. (7) All VAT liabilities shall be computed using the FMV of the VA at the time of transaction and remitted in the currency of transaction.

heading: Stamp Duties
text: 6.3 Stamp Duties (1) Stamp duty applies to TOKEN to FIAT and FIAT to TOKEN transfers under item 33 of the Ninth Schedule to the NTA. (2) Where the transaction is facilitated through a VASP or other recognised intermediary, the VASP or intermediary shall deduct and remit the applicable stamp duty in accordance with procedures prescribed by the Service. (3) Where a VA is used to settle a transaction that independently attracts stamp duty under the NTA, the applicable duty on the underlying instrument shall remain payable. (4) Nothing in these Guidelines shall be construed as exempting any dutiable instrument from stamp duty merely because settlement is effected through a VA. (5) Payments for goods or services using VA are not dutiable except where the underlying transaction is independently dutiable under the instruments listed in the Ninth Schedule to the NTA. (6) Where a transaction is settled using VA, the applicable duty on the underlying instrument under the Ninth Schedule shall be chargeable on the instrument. (7) The stamp duty applicable on VA transfers and any other duty under the Ninth Schedule to the NTA are separate duties and both may apply to the same transaction. (8) The stamp duty obligation crystallises at the point of the TOKEN to FIAT or FIAT to TOKEN conversion in Nigeria and is not affected by the subsequent transmission of the token to an offshore recipient. (9) The duty is borne by the transferee of the token in every dutiable transaction. The stamp duty is withheld from the token credited to the transferee and does not reduce the fiat consideration payable under the transaction. (10) A VASP shall withhold the stamp duty in token units from the tokens credited to the transferee and remit the duty so withheld to the Service not later than the 15th and 30th of the month of transaction. text: 7.2 Non-Taxable Events The events listed in this paragraph do not, of themselves, constitute a taxable disposal or taxable supply but they may establish the cost base for future disposals.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/21: Guidelines on the Taxation of Virtual Assets
heading: Holding of Virtual Assets
text: 7.2.1 Holding of Virtual Assets The mere holding of a VA after acquisition shall not constitute a taxable event. Accordingly, any unrealised appreciation in the value of a VA shall not be subject to income tax until the occurrence of a taxable disposal.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/21: Guidelines on the Taxation of Virtual Assets
heading: Transfers Between Wallets
text: 7.2.2 Transfers Between Wallets The transfer of a VA between wallets owned and controlled by the same individual shall not constitute a disposal for income tax purposes, provided that there is no change in the beneficial ownership of the VA. This does not apply where the transfer involves a company, partnership, trust, unincorporated association or any other legal person, or where there is any change in beneficial ownership.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/21: Guidelines on the Taxation of Virtual Assets
heading: Staking Lock-Up
text: 7.2.3 Staking Lock-Up The transfer or commitment of a VA into a staking, validation or similar protocol solely for the purpose of participating in network operations shall not constitute a disposal and shall not give rise to income tax.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/21: Guidelines on the Taxation of Virtual Assets
heading: Minting of Non-Fungible Tokens
text: 7.2.4 Minting of Non-Fungible Tokens 12 | Pa ge The creation or minting of a Non-Fungible Token (NFT) shall not constitute income, a disposal of property or a taxable supply. Tax liability shall arise only upon the first sale, transfer or other disposal of the NFT for consideration.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/21: Guidelines on the Taxation of Virtual Assets
heading: Tokenisation of Real-World Assets
text: 7.2.5 Tokenisation of Real-World Assets The tokenisation of a real-world asset shall not, of itself, constitute a disposal of the underlying asset where there is no change in beneficial ownership. The conversion of ownership rights into digital tokens shall be regarded as a change in the form of ownership and shall not give rise to income tax.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/21: Guidelines on the Taxation of Virtual Assets
heading: Collateralised Loans
text: 7.2.6 Collateralised Loans The receipt of funds or other consideration under a loan secured by VA shall not constitute taxable income. Such receipt shall be treated as the creation of a liability and shall not give rise to a taxable gain.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/21: Guidelines on the Taxation of Virtual Assets
heading: Taxable Supply
text: 7.2.7 Taxable Supply The transfer of a VA does not in itself constitute a taxable supply and does not attract VAT.

heading: Central Bank Digital Currencies
text: 7.2.8 Central Bank Digital Currencies The eNaira and all CBDCs are excluded from the VA tax framework.

text: 9.0 VALUATION AND COMPUTATION OF TAXABLE GAINS

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/21: Guidelines on the Taxation of Virtual Assets
heading: The dollar-referenced gain computation
text: 9.1 The dollar-referenced gain computation

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/21: Guidelines on the Taxation of Virtual Assets
heading: The Rule
text: 9.1.1 The Rule (1) The income tax on gain arising from the disposal of VA in Category 1 is computed by reference to the USD value of the asset at acquisition and at disposal. Only the resulting dollar gain is then converted to Naira at the CBN/NAFEM rate on the disposal date for the purpose of determining the Naira tax liability. (2) Gains arising on disposal of VA in Category 2 are measured against the underlying pegged fiat currency and will in normal circumstances be nil or negligible.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/21: Guidelines on the Taxation of Virtual Assets
heading: The Computation Formula
text: 9.1.2 The Computation Formula Step 1 — Dollar cost base: The USD price of the asset at acquisition. a. For fiat acquisitions, total fiat paid divided by net token units received after stamp duty deduction, converted to dollars at the CBN/NAFEM rate on the acquisition date. b. For swap acquisitions: the dollar FMV of the asset received on the swap date. Step 2 — Dollar disposal proceeds. The USD price of the asset at disposal. a. For fiat disposals: Naira proceeds received divided by the CBN/NAFEM rate on the disposal date. b. For swap disposals: the dollar FMV of the asset received on the swap date. 16 | Pa ge Step 3 — Dollar gain or loss. Dollar disposal proceeds minus dollar cost base. If negative, this is a dollar loss available for annual netting under paragraph 9.4. Step 4 — Naira taxable gain. Multiply the dollar gain by the CBN/NAFEM rate on the disposal date. The resulting Naira figure is the assessable gain for income tax purposes. Step 5 — Token deducted at source. a. Apply the applicable WHT rate (paragraph 8.0) to the gross disposal proceeds expressed in token terms to determine the token quantity to be withheld by the VASP at source. b. WHT is computed on gross proceeds, not on the gain. c. The Naira equivalent of the withheld token at the CBN/NAFEM rate on the withholding date constitutes the taxpayer's WHT credit on the annual return. Illustration 2 — Disposal for fiat with dollar-referenced gain 1. User A acquires 0.985 BTC (net after stamp duty) by paying ₦1,000,000. CBN/NAFEM rate at acquisition = ₦1,000/$. 2. Dollar cost base = $1,000 (= ₦1,000,000 ÷ ₦1,000/$). 3. User A sells 0.985 BTC. Proceeds = ₦1,970,000. Rate at disposal = ₦1,500/$. 4. Dollar disposal proceeds = $1,313.33. Dollar gain = $313.33. 5. Taxable Naira gain = $313.33 × ₦1,500 = ₦470,000. The Naira depreciation component (₦500,000) is excluded from taxable income. 6. For comparison: Under a straight Naira-to-Naira computation (without the dollar-referenced methodology), the apparent gain would be ₦1,970,000 − ₦1,000,000 = ₦970,000. The difference of ₦500,000 represents the effect of Naira depreciation from ₦1,000/$ to ₦1,500/$ during the holding period. Only the real dollar gain of $313.33, converted at the disposal date rate, is assessable. Illustration 3 — TOKEN/TOKEN swap 1. User A acquired 2 ETH at $1,500 per ETH. Dollar cost base = 2 × $1,500 = $3,000. 17 | Pa ge 2. User A swaps 2 ETH for 0.1 BTC when ETH = $2,000 and BTC = $40,000. The swap is treated as a disposal of 2 ETH and an acquisition of 0.1 BTC. 3. The FMV of the ETH disposed of is 2 × US$2,000 = US$4,000. Accordingly, the gross disposal proceeds are US$4,000. 4. The gain on disposal is computed as follows — (i) Dollar disposal proceeds = US$4,000 (ii) Dollar cost base = US$3,000 (iii) Dollar gain = US$1,000

heading: Assets not in USD
text: 9.2 Assets not in USD (1) Where a token is not directly priced in USD, its dollar FMV is derived by converting through its primary trading pair at the transaction timestamp. For example, a token priced in Bitcoin is converted to dollars using the Bitcoin dollar price at that timestamp; a token priced in Ether is converted using the Ether dollar price. (2) All prices must be sourced from an aggregator approved by the Service. The Service shall publish on its website, and may update from time to time, the list of approved aggregators or valuation sources for the purposes of these Guidelines. (3) The USD remains the reference currency for all gain computations. (4) Where no verifiable market price exists in any trading pair, the taxpayer must document the valuation methodology and retain it for at least six years unless otherwise permitted by the Service.

heading: Fiat acquisitions
text:
9.3 Cost base
9.3.1 Fiat acquisitions 18 | Pa ge (1) The cost base per unit is the total fiat consideration paid divided by the net token units received after stamp duty deduction, converted to dollars at the CBN/NAFEM rate on the acquisition date. (2) Where the cost base per unit therefore exceeds the market price per unit by the stamp duty component, then the duty paid at acquisition is embedded in the cost base and is not separately deductible at disposal.

text: 9.3.2 TOKEN/TOKEN swap The cost base of the new token received is the dollar FMV of the token disposed of at the swap date, divided by the number of units of the new token received.

heading: Gratuitous receipts
text: 9.3.3 Gratuitous receipts (1) For gratuitous receipts including staking rewards, mining rewards, airdrops with a realisable FMV at receipt, hard forks and promotional tokens, the cost base is stepped up to the dollar FMV at the time of receipt, since the full receipt value is already assessable as income at that point. (2) For hard fork distributions with no realisable FMV at the date of receipt, the cost base is nil and the full disposal proceeds are taxable on first disposal, consistent with treatment under paragraph 9.6 (3) FIFO is the default cost base method, or Weighted Average Cost is accepted as an alternative where elected consistently from the commencement of VA activity and applied without interruption. A taxpayer shall not switch methods retrospectively.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/21: Guidelines on the Taxation of Virtual Assets
heading: Annual netting of gains and losses
text: 9.4 Annual netting of gains and losses (1) Gains and losses from all VA disposals in a year of assessment shall be computed in USD and netted at year-end. (2) Each disposal gain or loss shall first be computed in USD and then converted to Naira using the CBN/NAFEM exchange rate on the date of the transaction. (3) The resulting Naira amounts shall be aggregated to determine the net assessable income (or loss) from VA disposals for the year. (4) Tax withheld by VASPs shall be credited against the final tax liability, with any balance payable or refundable through the annual return. (5) VA losses may only be set off against VA gains. (6) Losses from non-VA activities shall not be offset against VA gains, and VA losses shall not be offset against non-VA income as provided under section 27 of the NTA. (7) Capital losses may be carried forward indefinitely and set off only against future VA gains. 19 | Pa ge (8) In the case of individuals, trading losses incurred in the course of a VA trading business shall be deductible subject to section 28 of the NTA while in the case of companies, trading losses shall be carried forward in accordance with the provisions of NTA. (9) Losses arising from transactions between connected persons shall be computed by reference to the FMV of the asset at the time of disposal, and not the actual consideration.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/21: Guidelines on the Taxation of Virtual Assets
heading: Special rules for certain transactions
text: 9.5 Special rules for certain transactions The following rules shall apply to specified VA transactions— (1) Stablecoins: Gains arising from the disposal of stablecoins shall be determined by reference to the underlying pegged fiat currency. No withholding tax shall apply to the disposal of stablecoins. Any taxable gain shall be reported through the self-assessment return. (2) Cross-border Transactions: The conversion of Naira into VAs for cross-border settlement shall not constitute a taxable disposal for the purpose of income tax. Any subsequent disposal of the VA shall be subject to the applicable tax provisions. (3) Employment and Professional Income: VAs received as employment income or emoluments, or professional fees shall be valued at their FMV on the date of receipt and taxed in accordance with the applicable provisions of the NTA. (4) Staking, Mining and DeFi Rewards: VAs received as staking rewards, mining rewards, liquidity rewards or other decentralised finance incentives shall constitute taxable income on the date of receipt. The value recognised as income shall become the acquisition cost of the asset. (5) Non-Fungible Tokens: Income derived by a creator from the sale of an NFT shall constitute business income. Gains arising from the disposal of an NFT held as an investment shall be taxed in accordance with these Guidelines.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/21: Guidelines on the Taxation of Virtual Assets
heading: Airdrop computation
text: 9.6 Airdrop computation (1) The taxable amount is the FMV of the received tokens in USD on the date of receipt, converted to Naira using the prevailing CBN/NAFEM exchange rate on that date. (2) The cost base of the received tokens is stepped up to the FMV at receipt to prevent double taxation on future disposal. (3) In the case of a hard fork, the cost base of the original tokens remains unchanged and is not reduced or apportioned. The new tokens acquire a separate cost base equal to their FMV on the date of receipt. 20 | Pa ge (4) Where no active market, observable bid price, or redemption mechanism exists at receipt, the taxable amount at receipt is nil. Tax is deferred until first disposal, at which point the full disposal proceeds (converted to Naira) are taxable with a nil cost base. (5) Taxpayers must document the absence of FMV at receipt and retain records for six (6) years. (6) Tokens with no identifiable issuer/origin, no realisable FMV, and no prospect of realisation attract no tax liability at receipt or on disposal (unless actual proceeds are received). (7) Sub-paragraphs (4) to (6) does not apply to airdrops or hard fork distributions which remain subject to the general rules, i.e. those with no observable FMV or that are effectively worthless, benefit from the deferred taxation rule.

heading: Wrapped Tokens and DeFi Receipt Tokens
text: 10.0 Wrapped Tokens and DeFi Receipt Tokens

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/21: Guidelines on the Taxation of Virtual Assets
heading: Wrapped tokens
text: 10.1 Wrapped tokens (1) The conversion of a VA into its wrapped equivalent, including the conversion of Bitcoin (BTC) into Wrapped Bitcoin (WBTC), shall not constitute a taxable disposal where — (a) the taxpayer retains the beneficial ownership of the underlying VA; (b) the wrapped token represents the same underlying asset; and (c) no consideration is received other than the wrapped token. (2) The acquisition cost and holding period of the original VA shall be carried over to the wrapped token. (3) The subsequent unwrapping or redemption of the wrapped token for the underlying VA shall likewise not constitute a taxable disposal.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/21: Guidelines on the Taxation of Virtual Assets
heading: DeFi receipt tokens
text: 10.2 DeFi receipt tokens (1) The deposit of a VA into a decentralised finance protocol in exchange for a receipt token, including the deposit of Ether (ETH) in exchange for stETH or similar receipt tokens, shall not constitute a taxable disposal where — (a) the receipt token represents the taxpayer's continuing interest in the deposited VA; (b) the taxpayer retains the beneficial ownership of the underlying asset; and (c) the transaction does not result in the realisation of value. 21 | Pa ge (2) The cost base and holding period of the underlying VA shall be transferred to the receipt token.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/21: Guidelines on the Taxation of Virtual Assets
heading: Subsequent disposal
text: 10.3 Subsequent disposal Where a wrapped token or DeFi receipt token is— (a) sold; (b) exchanged for another VA; (c) used as consideration for goods or services; or (d) otherwise disposed of in a transaction involving a change in beneficial ownership, the transaction shall constitute a taxable disposal, and the gain or loss shall be computed in accordance with these Guidelines.

document_title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/21: Guidelines on the Taxation of Virtual Assets
heading: Income from Wrapped Tokens and DeFi Protocols
text: 10.4 Income from Wrapped Tokens and DeFi Protocols (1) Income derived from wrapped tokens or DeFi receipt tokens, shall constitute taxable income on the date the taxpayer acquires unrestricted ownership or control of the income. (2) The FMV recognised as income shall constitute the acquisition cost of the VA received for the purpose of any subsequent disposal.

heading: Token-native remittance
text:
11.0 Remittance of tax
11.1 Token-native remittance (1) Income tax deducted at source and stamp duty shall be remitted to the Service in the originating token of the transaction. (2) VAT shall be remitted in the currency of transaction in all cases. (3) No intermediate Naira conversion is required at the point of withholding for income tax or stamp duty. (4) Naira translation for income tax purposes shall occur only once, at the annual tax return stage, using the CBN/NAFEM exchange rate applicable on each transaction date.

text:
Implementation Timeline on the Phased Rollout of the E-Invoicing & Electronic Fiscal System (EFS) Regime.

The Nigeria Revenue Service (NRS) hereby informs taxpayers, tax practitioners, and the general public of the phased rollout of its E-Invoicing & Electronic Fiscal System (EFS) also known as the Merchant Buyer Solution (MBS), in furtherance of its mandate to enhance tax administration, improve transparency, and promote voluntary compliance.

Following extensive consultations and engagements, the MBS officially went live on 1st August 2025 for Large Taxpayers. In recognition of operational and transitional considerations, the effective implementation for this category was subsequently extended to November 2025.

Prior to the official go-live, the NRS conducted a series of stakeholder engagement sessions across several sectors of the Large Taxpayer community, including tax consultants and professional bodies, culminating in a pilot phase deployment in January 2025.

Since the official go-live, significant progress has been recorded, with the onboarding of the majority of Large Taxpayers, many of whom have commenced the successful transmission of invoice data to the MBS platform.

Building on these achievements, and in line with Section 23 of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act (NTAA), which empowers the Service to deploy technology for the administration and collection of taxes, as well as Section 158 of the Nigeria Tax Act (NTA), which mandates taxpayers to implement the fiscalisation system deployed by the Service, the NRS hereby notifies the general public of the continuation of the phased rollout of the E-Invoicing Solution to other taxpayer segments, namely Medium Taxpayers and Emerging Taxpayers.

The phased rollout will be implemented in a structured manner, covering the following stages:

- Stakeholder Engagement
- Pilot Rollout
- Go-Live
- Post Go-Live Review
- Compliance Enforcement
Each phase will be guided by clearly defined timelines and annual turnover thresholds applicable to the respective taxpayer segments.

Taxpayers are advised to take note of their applicable category and timelines and are encouraged to actively participate in engagement and onboarding activities as communicated by the Service from time to time.

The NRS remains committed to working collaboratively with all stakeholders to ensure a smooth transition and the successful adoption of the E-Invoicing Solution.

For further information, guidelines, and updates, taxpayers are advised to visit: einvoice.nrs.gov.ng or contact designated support desks.

document_title: Nigerian Tax ID Portal Goes Live   Effective January 1, 2026
heading: Nigerian Tax ID Portal Goes Live   Effective January 1, 2026
text:
Nigerian Tax ID Portal Goes Live   Effective January 1, 2026

As part of ongoing efforts to modernize and streamline tax administration in Nigeria, the Joint Revenue Board (JRB) and the Nigerian Revenue Service (NRS) are pleased to announce the launch of the Nigerian Tax ID Portal.

What is the Tax ID?

The Tax Identification (Tax ID) is a unique, system-generated number assigned to all taxable persons in Nigeria for the purpose of tax administration.

•⁠  ⁠For individuals, the Tax ID is linked to their National Identification Number (NIN).

•⁠  ⁠For non-individuals (businesses and organizations), it is linked to their Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) registration number.

How to Retrieve Your Tax ID

Visit www.taxid.jtb.gov.ng or www.taxid.nrs.gov.ng

*For Individuals:

1. Click on the "Individual" tab on the homepage.

2. Select National Identification Number (NIN).

3. Enter your 11 digit NIN

4. Click on "Retrieve Tax ID"

5. Enter "First Name", "Last Name" and "Date of Birth" exactly as captured by NIMC.

6. Click "Continue"

7. The 13 digit Tax ID will be displayed.

For Non-Individuals (Registered Entities)

1. Click on the "Corporate" tab.

2. Select the appropriate organisation type.

3. Enter your CAC registration number, as applicable.

4. Click "Retrieve Tax ID"

5. The13 digit Tax ID will be displayed

It's that simple!

Key Information.

Effective Date: The use of the new Tax ID becomes effective from January 1, 2026, replacing previously issued TINs.

Purpose: The Tax ID is strictly for tax administration.

Security Assurance: The introduction of the Tax ID will not lead to bank account deductions or closures due to non-compliance.

Key Benefits

1. Unified identification for all taxpayers

2. Simplified access to tax-related services

3. Nationwide accessibility and ease of use

Availability

The Nigerian Tax ID Portal is now live and accessible to all taxpayers across Nigeria starting January 1, 2026.

For further assistance, taxpayers are encouraged to visit the portal or contact their nearest tax office.

COMMENCEMENT OF COMPLIANCE MONITORING FOR LARGE TAXPAYERS UNDER THE NATIONAL E-INVOICING & ELECTRONIC FISCAL SYSTEM (EFS) REGIME

The Nigeria Revenue Service (NRS) wishes to remind all large taxpayers of the Public Notice issued on 17 February 2026 regarding the implementation timeline and mandatory adoption of the National E-Invoicing & Electronic Fiscal System (EFS), also known as the Merchant Buyer Solution (MBS).

As communicated in the Notice, all large taxpayers are required to complete the process of onboarding, integration, testing, and commence invoice transmission to the NRS E-Invoicing platform in accordance with the prescribed implementation framework.

The Service hereby notifies all affected taxpayers that it has commenced compliance monitoring activities to assess the level of adherence to the E-Invoicing mandate across the large taxpayer segment.

Accordingly, all large taxpayers that are yet to commence or complete implementation processes are required to ensure full compliance on or before 31 July 2026.

For the avoidance of doubt, compliance includes:

Completion of onboarding on the NRS Merchant Buyer Solution (MBS);

Successful integration of taxpayer systems through approved Access Point Providers (APPs) and/or Systems Integrators (SIs);

Completion of all required validation and testing activities; and

Active transmission of invoices to the NRS E-Invoicing platform in line with approved standards and guidelines;

Ensure you receive only compliant e-invoices with a valid Invoice Reference Number (IRN) from suppliers.

Affected taxpayers are therefore advised to urgently conclude all outstanding onboarding and integration activities and commence invoice transmission before the compliance deadline, failing which regulatory and enforcement actions will be triggered in accordance with the provisions of the relevant tax laws and regulations.

Visit: www.einvoice.nrs.gov.ng

heading: Collaboration key to successful implementation of new tax laws---FIRS chairman
text:
Collaboration key to successful implementation of new tax laws---FIRS chairman

Chairman of the Federal Inland Revenue Service (FIRS), Zacc Adedeji, has identified cooperation and collaboration among key stakeholders, including taxpayers and subnational governments, as crucial to the hitch-free implementation of the new tax laws.

Adedeji noted that FIRS, which is transitioning to the Nigeria Revenue Service (NRS), cannot in isolation bring about the success envisaged with the new laws, calling on the private sector, institutions and agencies across all levels to join hands to achieve the desired outcome.

This was just as the chairman of the Presidential Fiscal Policy and Tax Reforms Committee, Mr. Taiwo Oyedele, said the country was no longer where it was before the advent of President Bola Tinubu-led administration in terms of gloomy economic outlook.

A statement by Dare Adekanmbi, Special Adviser on Media to the FIRS chairman said the duo spoke in Abuja on Monday at a special engagement session organised for directors in the tax agency by the Committee and held at Abuja Continental Hotel.

The FIRS chairman expressed the readiness to position the tax agency as a partner in development working with all critical stakeholders to achieve the desired outcomes for the country by ensuring that the laws and tax policies are implemented fairly, consistently and transparently.

“Our collective posture should be one of readiness to listen, adapt and deliver…A key pillar of the reforms is capacity building. The demands of modern tax administration, from digitalisation, to data-driven compliance, cross-border taxation, and specialised industries, require new skills and approaches.

“As directors, you will lead the charge in equipping our officers with the knowledge, tools, and confidence to implement the law effectively, while providing support to taxpayers,” he said.

He promised to ensure the agency invests “in training, technology, and systems that enhance efficiency, reduce compliance costs, and strengthen trust in the system.”

Oyedele, in his opening remarks, reiterated that the country was no longer where it used to be according to the latest economic indices, stressing that the gains of the reforms were already yielding positive macro results.

Going to the specifics, he said the country’s balance of trade remains surplus from the deficit that it was before May 2023, just as he said the country is no longer printing money to meet its needs.

He added that the Tinubu-led administration had cleared unmet forex backlog, improved external reserves to $23billion in just two years, with the economic outlook set to be more robust going forward.

heading: Nigeria’s tax reforms get African Tax Administration Forum nod
text:
Nigeria’s tax reforms get African Tax Administration Forum nod

Africa must be on the table in global agenda, says FIRS chairman

The African Tax Administration Forum (ATAF) has thrown its weight behind Nigeria’s tax reforms which culminated in the new tax laws, describing them as necessary for economic growth and development.

The recently-inaugurated Executive Secretary of the continental body, Ms Mary Baine, made the support known during a visit to the chairman, Federal Inland Revenue Service (FIRS), Zacch Adedeji, in Abuja, on Tuesday.

A statement by Dare Adekanmbi, Special Adviser on Media to the FIRS chairman said ATAF stands by Nigeria in reforming its fiscal landscape and pledged the readiness of the body to give technical support in areas that would help in realising the gains of the reforms.

She referenced how the organization had helped Zambia to build capacity in the area of raising revenue from mining, promising to offer support to Nigeria in the same area.

According to her, ATAF is willing to leverage Nigeria’s continental and global influence to mobilise member-countries to strengthen the organisation.

“When you look at the strategic vision of FIRS, we see the things you are doing and the way you're changing the tax system, the kind of reforms and the time that it has taken and of course the movement forward.

“So, we applaud you, and I wanted to say that ATAF is here to say that we stand with you, we applaud you, and we're ready to provide whatever support that could lead to its success.

“In terms of your strategic vision— people, technology and data, we find that this is something that is really critical for the rest of the continent and that it is an area where ATAF will be happy to support as well,” she said.

The FIRS chairman, while welcoming the visitors, expressed confidence in the capacity of the Executive Secretary to lead ATAF to glory.

He charged Africans to look inwards for homegrown solutions to challenges, stressing that salvation cannot come from the Western world.

“My belief has always been that solutions to Africa’s challenges can only come from Africa. There is no free lunch anywhere. I have said that I don't believe in aids; I believe in cooperation.

"There is a saying that when you are not on the table, you are definitely on the menu. So, Africa must be on the table and that is it. We should stop being on the menu. That is my charge to you.

“So, the expectation from us as a continent is also to bring what we can contribute to the work, most especially in tax matters.  For us, we have to evolve our own fiscal policies which is what Nigeria has done with the new tax laws.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What is the Nigeria Revenue Service (NRS)?
text:
Q: What is the Nigeria Revenue Service (NRS)?
A: The Nigeria Revenue Service (NRS) is the successor institution to the Federal Inland Revenue Service (FIRS), as established under the Nigeria Revenue Service (Establishment) Act, 2025. It is established to modernise Nigeria’s domestic revenue administration, strengthen governance, expand the use of digital systems, and improve efficiency, transparency, and taxpayer service delivery.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: Why did FIRS transition to NRS?
text:
Q: Why did FIRS transition to NRS?
A: The transition was completed to establish the Nigerian Revenue Service (NRS) as a unified, modern revenue authority that aligns Nigeria’s revenue administration with global best practices, strengthens accountability, broadens the revenue base, and supports sustainable national development.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What are the core differences in mandate, scope, and structure between FIRS and NRS?
text:
Q: What are the core differences in mandate, scope, and structure between FIRS and NRS?
A: - Mandate: While FIRS focused primarily on tax administration, NRS has a broader mandate covering tax administration, non-tax revenues, digital compliance systems, and enhanced coordination across the revenue ecosystem, in line with the applicable Acts.
- Scope: NRS integrates tax administration with data analytics, e-invoicing, third-party information reporting, and stronger inter-agency collaboration.
- Structure: NRS operates under an enhanced and service-oriented governance framework, with clearer accountability and taxpayer protection mechanisms.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: How will intergovernmental coordination be affected?
text:
Q: How will intergovernmental coordination be affected?
A: Coordination with Ministries, Departments and Agencies (MDAs), State Governments, and other public institutions will continue seamlessly. Under NRS, collaboration frameworks are strengthened to promote harmonisation, information sharing, and the reduction of multiple taxation.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: Do taxpayers need to re-register or obtain new Tax Identification Numbers (TINs)?
text:
Q: Do taxpayers need to re-register or obtain new Tax Identification Numbers (TINs)?
A: No.

All existing taxpayer registrations, TINs, and records issued under FIRS remain valid and will migrate seamlessly to NRS systems.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: Will there be disruptions to tax filing, payment, audits, or refunds?
text:
Q: Will there be disruptions to tax filing, payment, audits, or refunds?
A: No significant disruption is anticipated. Extensive transition planning, systems testing, and phased implementation arrangements are in place to ensure business continuity before, during, and after the transition.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What benefits should taxpayers expect under NRS?
text:
Q: What benefits should taxpayers expect under NRS?
A: Taxpayers should expect improved service delivery, upgraded and more reliable digital platforms, enhanced guidance and public notices, and improved processing refunds mechanisms.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: How will taxpayer rights be protected under NRS?
text:
Q: How will taxpayer rights be protected under NRS?
A: Taxpayer rights, confidentiality, and due process remain fundamental principles. These are reinforced through stronger governance arrangements, improved data protection standards, clearer procedures, and the establishment of an independent Tax Ombudsman Office.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: Will existing audits, rulings, objections, and disputes remain valid?
text:
Q: Will existing audits, rulings, objections, and disputes remain valid?
A: Yes. All ongoing audits, advance rulings, objections, appeals, and dispute resolution processes continue uninterrupted and are assumed by NRS, pursuant to statutory succession and savings provisions, without restart or revalidation.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: Will engagement channels with tax practitioners change?
text:
Q: Will engagement channels with tax practitioners change?
A: Engagement channels will be enhanced rather than diminished. NRS will continue structured consultations, issue public notices and guidance, and maintain professional forums for dialogue.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: Will compliance procedures change?
text:
Q: Will compliance procedures change?
A: Any procedural enhancements will be communicated clearly and in advance, with appropriate transition periods to allow taxpayers and practitioners to adjust.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: Will tax collection, remittance, and reporting processes change as a result of the transition?
text:
Q: Will tax collection, remittance, and reporting processes change as a result of the transition?
A: Existing processes remain valid at transition. Any system or process enhancements will be introduced gradually and communicated well in advance.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: Will existing payment platforms and system integrations remain operational?
text:
Q: Will existing payment platforms and system integrations remain operational?
A: Yes. All current integrations and payment platforms will continue, subject to controlled upgrades, cybersecurity safeguards, and system optimisation.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: How does NRS align with international best practices?
text:
Q: How does NRS align with international best practices?
A: NRS is designed to reflect international standards in governance, transparency, digitalisation, risk-based compliance, and institutional autonomy.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: Will existing Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) and partnerships remain valid?
text:
Q: Will existing Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) and partnerships remain valid?
A: Yes. Existing agreements, MoUs, and partnerships remain valid in accordance with their terms, and applicable legal and regulatory frameworks.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: How does NRS handle data protection, confidentiality, and sovereignty?
text:
Q: How does NRS handle data protection, confidentiality, and sovereignty?
A: NRS applies strict data protection, confidentiality, and cybersecurity standards consistent with Nigerian law, including the Nigeria Data Protection Regulation (NDPR), and aligned with international norms.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: How does the transition promote transparency and accountability?
text:
Q: How does the transition promote transparency and accountability?
A: NRS is structured to strengthen transparency, accountability, and public trust through improved governance, clearer reporting, and enhanced public communication.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: Will the public experience service disruption?
text:
Q: Will the public experience service disruption?
A: No significant disruption is expected, and contingency measures are in place to address any operational issues that may arise during the transition.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: How will stakeholders and the public be kept informed?
text:
Q: How will stakeholders and the public be kept informed?
A: Through official announcements, media briefings, stakeholder engagements, public notices, and digital communication platforms.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What happens on 1 January 2026?
text:
Q: What happens on 1 January 2026?
A: On this date, NRS formally takes over operational responsibility for federation revenue administration in line with the expanded mandate. All statutory functions continue without interruption, in accordance with the commencement and transitional provisions of the relevant Acts.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What should stakeholders expect after transition?
text:
Q: What should stakeholders expect after transition?
A: •	Operational continuity

•	Improved taxpayer engagement and service delivery

•	Gradual system and process enhancements

•	Ongoing consultation with stakeholders

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What should stakeholders do if they experience transition-related challenges?
text:
Q: What should stakeholders do if they experience transition-related challenges?
A: Stakeholders may engage the NRS through official communication channels, tax offices, helpdesks, or stakeholder engagement platforms, and any disputes or grievances shall be addressed in accordance with the relevant Acts.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: Will there be new procurement opportunities under NRS?
text:
Q: Will there be new procurement opportunities under NRS?
A: All procurement activities will continue to comply strictly with the Public Procurement Act and Bureau of Public Procurement guidelines. Over time, new opportunities may arise in line with NRS’s modernisation agenda, following due process.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What is the Nigeria Tax Act 2025?
text:
Q: What is the Nigeria Tax Act 2025?
A: The Nigeria Tax Act 2025 is a unified tax legislation that consolidates and repeals multiple pre-existing tax laws, providing a single legal framework for the taxation of income, transactions, and financial instruments in Nigeria. It aims to simplify tax administration, enhance compliance, and align with modern fiscal policies.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: Why was this Act necessary?
text:
Q: Why was this Act necessary?
A: Historically, Nigeria’s tax system has been governed by multiple standalone laws that were frequently and inconsistently amended, resulting in overlaps, contradictions, and duplications. The Nigeria Tax Act 2025 establishes a single definitive reference point for all taxation rules. By incorporating provisions that are responsive to the growing digital economy, the Act also ensures that taxation is applied fairly and uniformly across all industries, without discrimination.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: When does the Act take effect?
text:
Q: When does the Act take effect?
A: The Act commences on 1st January 2026.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: Which previous tax laws are repealed by this Act?
text:
Q: Which previous tax laws are repealed by this Act?
A: The Act repeals several laws including the Capital Gains Tax Act, Companies Income Tax Act, Personal Income Tax Act, Value Added Tax Act, Stamp Duties Act, Petroleum Profits Tax Act, and others listed in Section 196.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: Which previous tax laws are not repealed by this Act?
text:
Q: Which previous tax laws are not repealed by this Act?
A: Laws governing administration, institutions, customs, sector-specific levies, and subnational taxation.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: Who is subject to tax under this Act?
text:
Q: Who is subject to tax under this Act?
A: The Act applies to any person required to comply with tax laws in Nigeria, whether personally or on behalf of another, including individuals, companies, partnerships, trustees, and non-residents with economic presence in Nigeria.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What is considered taxable income?
text:
Q: What is considered taxable income?
A: Taxable income includes profits from trade or business, employment income, dividends, interest, royalties, gains from disposal of assets (including digital assets), and income from trusts, estates, and partnerships (Section 4).

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: How are non-residents taxed?
text:
Q: How are non-residents taxed?
A: Non-residents are taxed on income derived from Nigeria, especially if they have a permanent establishment or significant economic presence in Nigeria (e.g., digital services, e-commerce). Withholding tax may apply as a final tax in some cases.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What is “Significant Economic Presence”?
text:
Q: What is “Significant Economic Presence”?
A: A non-resident is deemed to have a significant economic presence if they transmit signals, sounds, messages, images, or data to Nigeria for activities such as e-commerce, digital content, online advertising, cloud computing, etc., and profit is attributable to such activities (Section 17(9)(b)).

Profits or gains from transactions in digital or virtual assets (cryptocurrencies etc) are taxable under the Act (Section 4(1)(j)).

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What is the tax rate for individuals?
text:
Q: What is the tax rate for individuals?
A: Individual income tax rates are specified in the Fourth Schedule and apply to chargeable income after allowable deductions (Section 58).

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: How is employment income defined?
text:
Q: How is employment income defined?
A: Employment income includes salaries, wages, allowances, bonuses, benefits-in-kind, and other perquisites (Section 13).

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What are the tax rates for companies?
text:
Q: What are the tax rates for companies?
A: 	Small companies: 0%

	Other companies: 30% (to be reduced to 25% by presidential order)

	Minimum effective tax rate of 15% for certain large companies (Sections 56–57).

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What is the Development Levy?
text:
Q: What is the Development Levy?
A: A 4% development levy is imposed on assessable profits of companies (excluding small and non-resident companies). Proceeds are allocated to funds such as Tertiary Education Trust Fund, Nigerian Education Loan, Cybersecurity Fund, etc. (Section 59).

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What is the tax treatment of benefits-in-kind?
text:
Q: What is the tax treatment of benefits-in-kind?
A: Benefits-in-kind are valued at 5% of the employer’s acquisition cost or market value, or the annual rent/hire cost, and are taxable in the hands of the employee (Section 14).

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What incentives are available for priority sectors?
text:
Q: What incentives are available for priority sectors?
A: Priority sectors listed in the Tenth Schedule may qualify for Economic Development Tax Incentives, including tax credits and exemptions for up to 5 years (Sections 166–184).

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What is the VAT rate under the new Act?
text:
Q: What is the VAT rate under the new Act?
A: VAT is charged at 7.5% on taxable supplies, with exemptions and zero-rating for certain items (Sections 148, 186–187).

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What VAT supplies are zero-rated?
text:
Q: What VAT supplies are zero-rated?
A: Zero-rated supplies include basic food items, medical and pharmaceutical products, educational materials, agricultural equipment, and exported goods and services (except oil and gas) (Sections 186–187).

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: Who is required to register for a Taxpayer Identification Number (Tax ID)?
text:
Q: Who is required to register for a Taxpayer Identification Number (Tax ID)?
A: Every taxable person, including individuals, companies, ministries, departments, agencies (MDAs), and non-residents supplying goods or services in Nigeria, must register with the relevant tax authority and obtain a Tax ID.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What taxes are administered by the Nigeria Revenue Service (NRS)?
text:
Q: What taxes are administered by the Nigeria Revenue Service (NRS)?
A: The NRS administers taxes on companies, non-resident persons, petroleum operations, value-added tax (VAT), surcharge on fossil fuels, stamp duties, and certain other taxes as specified in Section 3 of the Act.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What are the penalties for failing to register for tax?
text:
Q: What are the penalties for failing to register for tax?
A: A taxable person who fails to register may face an administrative penalty of ₦50,000 for the first month and ₦25,000 for each subsequent month of default.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: When must companies file their annual tax returns?
text:
Q: When must companies file their annual tax returns?
A: Companies must file self-assessment returns within six months after the end of their accounting year. Newly incorporated companies must file within 18 months of incorporation or six months after their first accounting period, whichever is earlier.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: Are there special filing requirements for Virtual Asset Service Providers (VASPs)?
text:
Q: Are there special filing requirements for Virtual Asset Service Providers (VASPs)?
A: Yes. VASPs must submit monthly returns detailing transactions, customer information, and asset values to the relevant tax authority, in addition to standard annual returns.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What happens if I fail to file a tax return on time?
text:
Q: What happens if I fail to file a tax return on time?
A: Late filing may result in penalties, interest on unpaid tax, and possible prosecution. Specific penalties vary by tax type and duration of default.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: Can tax assessments be disputed?
text:
Q: Can tax assessments be disputed?
A: Yes. Taxpayers may object to an assessment within 30 days of receiving the notice by submitting a written objection to the relevant tax authority, stating the grounds for dispute.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What is the role of the State Internal Revenue Service (SIRS)?
text:
Q: What is the role of the State Internal Revenue Service (SIRS)?
A: The SIRS assesses and collects taxes from individuals, estates, trusts, and businesses within the state, in accordance with the Act and state laws.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What is the National Single Window Portal?
text:
Q: What is the National Single Window Portal?
A: It is a digital platform established by the Law to streamline import/export processes, enhance revenue assurance, and improve transparency in trade and tax administration.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: How are VAT revenues distributed among governments?
text:
Q: How are VAT revenues distributed among governments?
A: VAT revenue is distributed as follows: 10% to the Federal Government, 55% to State Governments and the FCT, and 35% to Local Governments, based on equality, population, and consumption.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What are the penalties for non-remittance of withheld taxes?
text:
Q: What are the penalties for non-remittance of withheld taxes?
A: Failure to remit deducted taxes may result in a penalty of 10% per annum on the amount not remitted, plus interest at the prevailing Central Bank monetary policy rate.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: Can a tax agent represent a taxpayer?
text:
Q: Can a tax agent represent a taxpayer?
A: Yes, but the agent must be accredited by the relevant tax authority. Returns filed by unaccredited agents may not be considered duly filed.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What is an Advance Ruling and how can it be obtained?
text:
Q: What is an Advance Ruling and how can it be obtained?
A: An Advance Ruling is a binding decision issued by the tax authority on the interpretation of tax laws for a specific transaction. Taxpayers may apply in the prescribed form and receive a response within 21 days.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What records must be kept for tax purposes?
text:
Q: What records must be kept for tax purposes?
A: Taxpayers must maintain books of account in English or with a certified translation, and retain them for at least six years after the relevant assessment year.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What powers do tax authorities have during investigations?
text:
Q: What powers do tax authorities have during investigations?
A: Authorized officers may access premises, inspect records, remove documents, and with a warrant, enter private dwellings. They may also seek police assistance for enforcement.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What constitutes a “small business” under the Act?
text:
Q: What constitutes a “small business” under the Act?
A: A small business is one with an annual turnover of ₦100 million or less and total fixed assets below ₦250 million, excluding professional service providers.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: Are there special tax rules for the petroleum and mining sectors?
text:
Q: Are there special tax rules for the petroleum and mining sectors?
A: Yes. The Act includes specific return, assessment, and payment rules for upstream petroleum operations, LNG operations, and mineral royalty payments, with  penalties for non-compliance.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What is the penalty for obstructing a tax officer?
text:
Q: What is the penalty for obstructing a tax officer?
A: Obstruction of an authorized officer may result in an administrative penalty of ₦1 million and/or imprisonment for up to three years.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: How are tax refunds processed?
text:
Q: How are tax refunds processed?
A: Refunds may be claimed within six years of the relevant assessment year. VAT refunds must be claimed within 12 months of the transaction. Refunds are typically processed within 90 days of approval.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: Is there a special return for those in the informal sector?
text:
Q: Is there a special return for those in the informal sector?
A: Yes, they are allowed to file simplified returns based on the guideline provided by the relevant tax authority.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What is the Nigeria Revenue Service (NRS)?
text:
Q: What is the Nigeria Revenue Service (NRS)?
A: The Nigeria Revenue Service (NRS) is a statutory body established by the NRS (Establishment) Act, 2025, to replace the Federal Inland Revenue Service (FIRS). It is responsible for the assessment, collection, and accounting of revenues due to the Government of the federation.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: How are chargeable gains computed?
text:
Q: How are chargeable gains computed?
A: Chargeable gains are computed as disposal proceeds less acquisition cost and incidental expenses, with specific rules for part-disposals, losses, and replacements (Sections 33–55).

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: Are gifts subject to tax?
text:
Q: Are gifts subject to tax?
A: Gifts are generally not subject to tax, except where the asset was acquired by way of gift and disposed of for consideration (Section 54).

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: How is rental income taxed?
text:
Q: How is rental income taxed?
A: Rental income is included in taxable income and may be subject to deductions for repairs, interest, and other expenses (Section 4).

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What is the tax treatment of collective investment schemes?
text:
Q: What is the tax treatment of collective investment schemes?
A: Collective investment schemes are treated as companies for tax purposes, with income taxable at the scheme level and distributions taxed in the hands of unit holders (Section 63).

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: How are exports taxed?
text:
Q: How are exports taxed?
A: Profits from exported goods and services are exempt from income tax if proceeds are repatriated through official channels (Section 163).

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What is the tax credit for research and development?
text:
Q: What is the tax credit for research and development?
A: Companies may deduct up to 5% of turnover for research and development expenses incurred in Nigeria (Section 165).

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: How does the Act address double taxation?
text:
Q: How does the Act address double taxation?
A: The Act provides for unilateral relief and recognition of double taxation agreements to avoid double taxation on foreign-sourced income (Sections 120–123).

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: How is unilateral relief of double taxation claimed?
text:
Q: How is unilateral relief of double taxation claimed?
A: A Nigeria resident whose income has been subject to tax in a foreign land may claim a relief for such tax to the limit of the applicable tax rate in Nigeria and within the time frame allowed under the law (Sections 120–123).

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: How are digital service providers taxed?
text:
Q: How are digital service providers taxed?
A: Non-resident digital service providers with significant economic presence in Nigeria are subject to income tax and VAT on Nigerian-sourced income (Sections 17, 151).

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What records must be maintained for tax purposes?
text:
Q: What records must be maintained for tax purposes?
A: Taxable persons must maintain accurate records, including invoices, receipts, contracts, and financial statements, as required under the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: How are disputes with tax authorities resolved?
text:
Q: How are disputes with tax authorities resolved?
A: Disputes may be resolved through objections, appeals, and other administrative processes as provided in the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025 and referenced in various sections of this Act.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What is the purpose of the Joint Revenue Board (JRB) of Nigeria Act, 2025?
text:
Q: What is the purpose of the Joint Revenue Board (JRB) of Nigeria Act, 2025?
A: The Act establishes the Joint Revenue Board, the Tax Appeal Tribunal, and the Office of the Tax Ombud to harmonize, coordinate, and settle disputes arising from revenue administration in Nigeria.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: Which previous tax laws are repealed by the JRB Establishment Act
text:
Q: Which previous tax laws are repealed by the JRB Establishment Act
A: Section 86 of the Personal Income Tax Act.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What are the key institutions established under the Act?
text:
Q: What are the key institutions established under the Act?
A: •	The Joint Revenue Board (JRB)

•	The Tax Appeal Tribunal (TAT)

•	The Office of the Tax Ombud

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: Who chairs the Joint Revenue Board?
text:
Q: Who chairs the Joint Revenue Board?
A: The Chairman is the Executive Chairman of the Nigeria Revenue Service.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: Who are the members of the Joint Revenue Board?
text:
Q: Who are the members of the Joint Revenue Board?
A: Members include:

	Chairmen of all State Internal Revenue Services and the FCT IRS

	Representatives from:

	Ministry of Finance

	National Identity Management Commission

	Revenue Mobilisation, Allocation and Fiscal Commission

	Nigerian Immigration Service

	Federal Road Safety Corps

	Nigeria Customs Service

	Nigeria Revenue Service

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: What are the main functions of the Joint Revenue Board?
text:
Q: What are the main functions of the Joint Revenue Board?
A: Key functions include:

	Maintaining a national taxpayer database

	Resolving disputes between tax authorities

	Advising on double taxation and tax policy

	Promoting tax harmonization across Nigeria

	Publishing tax revenue and expenditure data

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: Where is the head office of the Joint Revenue Board located?
text:
Q: Where is the head office of the Joint Revenue Board located?
A: The head office is in the Federal Capital Territory, Abuja.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: Who appoints members of the Tax Appeal Tribunal?
text:
Q: Who appoints members of the Tax Appeal Tribunal?
A: Members (Tax Appeal Commissioners) are appointed by the Minister of Finance.

document_title: NRS Frequently Asked Questions (nrs.gov.ng)
heading: How long is the term of a Tax Appeal Commissioner?
text:
Q: How long is the term of a Tax Appeal Commissioner?
A: The term is three years, renewable for another three years only.

heading: What is the Office of the Tax Ombud?   Drag
